content: The University of Fribourg, located in the city of Fribourg, Switzerland, was officially established in 1889 by Georges Python, a local businessman. However, its roots can be traced back to 1580 with the founding of the Jesuit Seminary of St. Michel. The university offers courses in both French and German, and students are generally expected to have proficiency in both languages, except in certain departments like history and law, where bilingual curricula are available. The university has approximately 10,000 students and traditionally attracts a significant number of students from the Italian-speaking region of Ticino. The Misericorde Campus, built between 1939 and 1942, was designed by architects Honegger and Dumas, who were students of the renowned Swiss architect Le Corbusier, making the campus architecturally significant. The university comprises five faculties: Catholic theology, law, natural sciences, arts, and economics and social sciences. The university's origins are tied to the Jesuit College St. Michel, founded in 1580 by St. Pierre Canisius on Belze Hill at the invitation of the Fribourg government. The establishment of Catholic higher education was a response to the rise of Protestant academies in Geneva, Lausanne, and Basel. In 1763, an Academy of Law was created, housed in the Albertinium, which is now a Dominican residence. The cantonal library was established in 1834, incorporating works from Catholic monasteries. After the Jesuits were expelled from Fribourg following the Sonderbund War, the College St. Michel was closed. In 1886, Georges Python, a prominent figure in Fribourg politics and education, became Director of Public Education. He secured funding for the university through a lottery and a grant of 2.5 million CHF from the canton. Initially, lectures were held in the buildings of St. Michel, and the cantonal library was integrated into the university. The Academy of Law evolved into the Faculty of Law, and the theological faculty was managed by the Dominicans under an agreement with the canton. By 1939, the university moved to the Misericorde campus due to overcrowding at St. Michel, which was then repurposed as a gymnasium. The Perolles campus was later constructed on the site of a former wagon factory. The city itself is predominantly French-speaking (70%), which has influenced the university's administration and student union. In recent years, the university completed the construction of its Perolles 2 campus, which now houses the Faculty of Economics and Social Sciences. Plans are underway to build a Museum for Biblical Antiquities in the Tower of Henry IV after its renovation. The university has also established FriMat, a center of excellence in nanotechnology. As part of the BeNeFri association, which includes the Universities of Bern, Neuchâtel, and Fribourg, students can take courses at any of the member universities and receive credit at their home institution. The university has transitioned to the Bologna process, awarding Bachelor's degrees after three years and Master's degrees after an additional two years. The university does not have a centralized campus, with its buildings spread across the city. Key sites include Misericorde (humanities and central administration), Perolles (science), Perolles 2 (economics), Regina Mundi (psychology), BCU centrale (main library), Pierre Aeby (classical philology), Bonnesfontaines (pedagogy), and Stade St. Leonard (university stadium). The university has several traditions. The Dies Academicus, held annually in November, begins with a Mass in the Chapel of the Collège St. Michel, followed by a procession to the Aula Magna (Great Hall), where honorary degrees are awarded after speeches by the rector and a guest speaker. Student guilds, similar to those at Scandinavian universities, are organized along geographic and linguistic lines. They dine together weekly in uniform and historically engaged in dueling. Membership in these guilds has been advantageous for careers in business, politics, and law. The Day of Welcomes (Jour d'Accueil) is akin to Freshers' Week, where new students are welcomed by the rector and the city's mayor, followed by a communal meal at the university Mensa. Student life at the university includes sports such as skiing, fencing, ice hockey, football, and basketball. Unlike many universities, Fribourg does not have its own student residences. Most students rent private accommodations, although some live in foyers run by religious organizations, such as Cité St. Justin and the Salesianum. A student housing cooperative, REST, also exists. The university used to award a Lizenziat (equivalent to a Master's degree) after five or five and a half years of study, but now follows the Bologna system. Students maintain a tabella, a booklet where professors sign off on attended lectures. Fribourg has a vibrant nightlife, with popular bars like Café Populaire and clubs such as Fri-Son, which hosts renowned musical acts. The university's seal features a cross and bishop's ring, symbolizing its Catholic heritage, on a black-and-white shield representing the canton of Fribourg. A modern blue logo with triangles symbolizing the Alps is increasingly used. Notable alumni and faculty include writers, academics, clergy, politicians, business leaders, architects, and media figures. Among them are philosopher Emmanuel Levinas, mathematician Michel Plancherel, Swiss President Joseph Deiss, and U.S. Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia. Trivia about the university includes the fact that Benito Mussolini once worked as a stonemason on its central library. The university holds the third-largest collection of Biblical antiquities in the world, after the British Museum and the Cairo Museum. During World War II, it organized educational camps for Polish prisoners of war. The Catholic Church in Switzerland collects funds annually on Fribourg Sunday to provide scholarships for foreign priests studying theology at the university. To commemorate its centenary, a stamp featuring the figures of Science and Wisdom was issued by La Poste.
